slides.title: What Is Inheritance?
slides.content: Inheritance lets one class (the derived class) reuse, extend, and modify the behavior of another class (the base class). It promotes code reuse and models 'is-a' relationships, like a Dog is an Animal. The derived class gets all the base class's fields and methods automatically.

exercise.prompt: If 'Dog : Animal', what relationship does this represent?

slides.title: The Base and Derived Classes
slides.content: The base class (or parent/superclass) is the class being inherited from. The derived class (or child/subclass) is the one doing the inheriting. In C#, you use the colon syntax: 'class Derived : Base'. A class can have only ONE base class (no multiple inheritance).

exercise.prompt: Which syntax correctly declares Car inheriting from Vehicle?

slides.title: Calling the Base Constructor
slides.content: When you create an object of the derived class, its constructor implicitly calls a base class constructor. You can use ': base(args)' to explicitly choose which base constructor runs. If the base class only has a parameterized constructor, you must call it explicitly.

exercise.prompt: To explicitly call a base class constructor, use ': _____' in the derived constructor declaration.

slides.title: Virtual and Override
slides.content: By default, a method in a derived class with the same name as a base method hides it (using 'new'). To truly override it—changing its behavior in the derived class—mark the base method 'virtual' and the derived method 'override'. This enables polymorphism.

exercise.prompt: Mark the Cat class's MakeSound method to override the base class version.
hints: Make sure your code includes the required keywords/elements: class, virtual, public
When run, your code should output: Meow

slides.title: Constructor Execution Order
slides.content: When you create a derived class object, initialization runs from the top down: base class field initializers and constructor first, then derived class field initializers and constructor body. This ensures the base object is fully formed before the derived class extends it.

exercise.prompt: Which runs first when you instantiate a derived class?

slides.title: Sealed Classes and Methods
slides.content: You can prevent a class from being inherited by marking it 'sealed'. You can also prevent a method from being overridden further by marking an override 'sealed'. This is useful for security and to preserve implementation invariants.

exercise.prompt: What keyword prevents a class from being inherited?

slides.title: Inheritance and Member Access
slides.content: A derived class inherits public, protected, internal, and protected internal members from its base class. Private members are inherited in the sense that they exist in the object, but they are not accessible by name from the derived class. Constructors are never inherited directly.

exercise.prompt: Private members from the base class are NOT accessible in the derived class because they have _____ access.

slides.title: The Object Class (Ultimate Base)
slides.content: Every class in C# implicitly inherits from the 'object' class. This means all classes have access to methods like ToString(), Equals(), and GetHashCode(). You can override these methods in your class to provide custom behavior.

exercise.prompt: Override ToString in the Person class to return 'Name: <name>'.
hints: Make sure your code includes the required keywords/elements: override, ToString
When run, your code should output: Name: Eve
